extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in humor theory (psychology/philosophy students and general educated readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and apply Schopenhauer's expectation-violation account of humor: that laughter arises from a sudden perception of incongruity between an idea/expectation and real events, including its proposed subtypes and limitations. Useful for analyzing what makes verbal/semantic phenomena (puns, similes) funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation-violation (Schopenhauer's core claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The cause of laughter in every case is simply the sudden perception of the incongruity between a concept and the real objects which have been thought through it in some relation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor arises from a sudden perception of incongruity between an idea/concept and the real-world object or event instantiated through that concept. This is the central criterion: a perceived mismatch between expectation (concept) and reality (event) produces laughter when recognized suddenly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity must be between event and pre-existing idea/expectation (not incongruity per se)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schopenhauer's refinement: it is not incongruity itself that is funny, but incongruity between an event in the world and a pre-existing idea or expectation about that event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish mere mismatch from expectation-violation: the audience must hold an expectation or concept which the event contradicts. Anti-pattern: invoking 'incongruity' without establishing an expectation (many mismatches do not produce mirth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual bifurcation (one-category-to-two-categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous bifurcation occurs when an idea thought to belong to one category turns out to belong to two categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical example: puns, where a word or phrase is reinterpreted to fit multiple categories simultaneously. Use when an initially single interpretation splits into two competing interpretations that both seem applicable, producing humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual subsumption (two-distinct-ideas-are-one)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous subsumption occurs when two ideas believed to be in distinct categories actually belong to the same category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in jokes that ask how one thing is like another — the humor comes from collapsing an assumed distinction. Use when disparate concepts are reclassified as the same, overturning expectations about their separateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ludicrous effect scales with size of the incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Schopenhauer suggested that the degree of funniness ('the ludicrous effect') is related to the size of the relevant incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bigger violations of expectation should produce greater humor (in principle). The author illustrates this with corpus-frequency intuition: less expected pairings (e.g. 'ghost llama') feel funnier than more expected ones (e.g. 'ghost cat'). Note: Schopenhauer proposed the relation but did not quantify it; empirical attempts are challenging and ongoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency/expectation modulation affects funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations formed by experience/frequency influence how large an incongruity is perceived to be and thus how funny it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical cue: word-pair occurrence rates (Google counts cited) suggest rarer collocations violate expectations more and can be perceived as funnier. Example given: 'ghost llama' (fewer occurrences) judged funnier than 'ghost cat' (many occurrences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Many incongruities produce non-humorous reactions (anti-patterns / limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all incongruities produce laughter; some evoke pain, anger, sadness, loathing, or other negative reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use caution: historical critics (e.g., Alexander Bain) catalogued many incongruities—corpse at a feast, parental cruelty, etc.—that are incongruous but elicit negative emotions rather than mirth. Any application of expectation-violation must account for emotional valence and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity and quantification caveat for real jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Real jokes often contain complex, multi-faceted incongruities that resist simple quantification or single-dimension measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: trying to reduce funniness to a single numeric 'size of incongruity' without accounting for layered, interacting sources of expectation-violation. The author notes practical difficulty extending simple frequency-based measures to full jokes.
